lesson.intro: A quadratic equation is any equation that can be put in the form $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ with $a\neq 0$. The Digital SAT asks about quadratics constantly: solve one, count how many real solutions it has, find the value of a parameter that makes it have exactly one solution, or read the answer out of a short story about a falling ball or a rectangular garden. There are only four tools --- factoring, square roots, completing the square and the quadratic formula --- and the whole game is choosing the fastest one for the equation in front of you.

blocks.title: The zero-product property and solving by factoring
blocks.body:
Everything about quadratics rests on one fact: if a product is zero, one of the factors is zero. So if $(x-2)(x+5)=0$, then $x-2=0$ or $x+5=0$, giving $x=2$ or $x=-5$. To use this, the equation must first be arranged with $0$ on one side. Given $x^{2}+3x=10$, do not divide by $x$ and do not guess --- move everything left, $x^{2}+3x-10=0$, then factor into $(x+5)(x-2)=0$.

When $a=1$, factoring $x^{2}+bx+c$ means finding two numbers whose product is $c$ and whose sum is $b$. For $x^{2}-7x+10$ the pair is $-2$ and $-5$: their product is $10$ and their sum is $-7$, so the factorisation is $(x-2)(x-5)$ and the roots are $2$ and $5$. Notice that the roots are the negatives of the numbers inside the parentheses; that sign flip is where most careless errors live.

blocks.title: Roots, zeros and $x$-intercepts are the same thing
blocks.body: The solutions of $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$, the zeros of the function $f(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$, and the $x$-coordinates of the points where the parabola $y=ax^{2}+bx+c$ crosses the $x$-axis are three names for one set of numbers. When a question says ``the graph of $y=x^{2}-6x+8$ intersects the $x$-axis at $(r,0)$ and $(s,0)$'', it is simply asking you to solve $x^{2}-6x+8=0$.

blocks.title: Square roots and completing the square
blocks.body:
If the equation contains no plain $x$ term --- only a perfect square and a constant --- take square roots directly and keep both signs: $(x-3)^{2}=49$ gives $x-3=\pm 7$, so $x=10$ or $x=-4$. Any quadratic can be forced into this shape by completing the square. Starting from $x^{2}+8x-3=0$, move the constant across to get $x^{2}+8x=3$, then add the square of half the coefficient of $x$, that is $(8/2)^{2}=16$, to both sides: $x^{2}+8x+16=19$, i.e. $(x+4)^{2}=19$, so $x=-4\pm\sqrt{19}$.

When the leading coefficient is not $1$, factor it out of the first two terms first. From $2x^{2}+12x+5=0$ write $2(x^{2}+6x)+5=0$, complete the square inside, $2\big[(x+3)^{2}-9\big]+5=0$, and tidy up to $2(x+3)^{2}=13$.

blocks.title: Formulas you must know
blocks.body:
For $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ with $a\neq 0$:
\[x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a},\qquad D=b^{2}-4ac.\]
The quantity $D$ is the discriminant, and it alone decides how many real solutions there are:
\[D>0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{two distinct real solutions},\quad D=0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{exactly one},\quad D<0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{none}.\]
Vieta's formulas give the sum and product of the two solutions without solving at all:
\[r_{1}+r_{2}=-\frac{b}{a},\qquad r_{1}r_{2}=\frac{c}{a}.\]
Finally, the vertex form $y=a(x-h)^{2}+k$ produced by completing the square has its vertex at $(h,k)$ and axis of symmetry $x=h=-\dfrac{b}{2a}$.

blocks.title: Choosing a method in five seconds
blocks.body: Scan the equation before you write anything. No $x$ term? Take square roots. Factors jump out (small integer coefficients, $a=1$)? Factor. Asked only for the sum or product of the solutions? Use Vieta and stop. Asked only how many solutions, or for a parameter that forces one solution? Use the discriminant and never solve. Asked to rewrite in the form $(x+h)^{2}=k$ or to find a vertex? Complete the square. Nothing else works? Quadratic formula.

blocks.title: Common traps
blocks.body:
Forgetting the $\pm$. $x^{2}=25$ has two solutions, $5$ and $-5$; a question that says ``the positive solution'' is warning you that there is another one.

Sign of the root. From $(x+6)(x-1)=0$ the roots are $-6$ and $1$, not $6$ and $-1$.

Dividing by $x$. Solving $x^{2}=5x$ by cancelling $x$ loses the solution $x=0$; factor as $x(x-5)=0$ instead.

Dividing wrongly by $2a$. In the quadratic formula the whole numerator, $-b$ included, sits over $2a$: $x=\dfrac{6\pm\sqrt{8}}{4}$ is not $6\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{8}}{4}$.

The discriminant is $b^{2}-4ac$, not $b^{2}+4ac$, and a negative $c$ makes $-4ac$ positive.

Answering the wrong question. In a word problem the algebra usually produces two roots and only one of them is a length or a time; a negative time is not an answer.

blocks.title: Calculator / strategy
blocks.body: On the calculator section you may graph $y=ax^{2}+bx+c$ in Desmos and read the $x$-intercepts straight off the curve; that also settles ``how many real solutions'' instantly. Even better, type the equation itself with a parameter and add a slider when a question asks for the value of $k$ that makes the graph touch the axis exactly once. If a question gives you four numerical choices, testing them is often faster than solving: substitute and see which one makes the equation true. And when the answer must be a single grid-in value, re-read the question --- the SAT usually wants the positive solution, the sum of the solutions, or a coefficient, precisely because those are single numbers.

blocks.title: Worked example 1 --- factoring versus Vieta
Worked example 2 --- a parameter and the discriminant
blocks.body:
\textbf{In the $xy$-plane, the line $y=2x+3$ intersects the parabola $y=x^{2}+k$ at exactly one point. What is the value of $k$?}

Set the expressions equal: $x^{2}+k=2x+3$, so $x^{2}-2x+(k-3)=0$. ``Exactly one point of intersection'' means this quadratic has exactly one real solution, so its discriminant is zero:
\[D=(-2)^{2}-4(1)(k-3)=4-4k+12=16-4k=0\ \Longrightarrow\ k=4.\]
Check: with $k=4$ the equation becomes $x^{2}-2x+1=(x-1)^{2}=0$, a single root $x=1$, and the point of tangency is $(1,5)$. Note that you never had to solve anything --- the discriminant answered a question about the number of solutions directly, which is exactly what it is for.

blocks.title: Worked example 3 --- a projectile
blocks.body:
\textbf{A ball is launched from a $24$-foot platform and its height in feet after $t$ seconds is $h=-16t^{2}+40t+24$. After how many seconds does it hit the ground?}

Hitting the ground means $h=0$: $-16t^{2}+40t+24=0$. Divide by $-8$ to keep the numbers clean: $2t^{2}-5t-3=0$, which factors as $(2t+1)(t-3)=0$, so $t=-\tfrac12$ or $t=3$. Time cannot be negative, so the ball lands after $3$ seconds. The rejected root is not a mistake --- it is the algebra's way of describing where the parabola would have crossed the axis before the launch.

problems.stem: What is the larger of the two solutions to $x^{2}-7x+10=0$?
problems.solution: Two numbers multiplying to $10$ and adding to $-7$ are $-2$ and $-5$, so the equation factors as $(x-2)(x-5)=0$. The zero-product property gives $x=2$ or $x=5$, and the question asks for the larger one. The distractors $7$ and $10$ are the coefficients themselves, which are the sum and product of the roots, not the roots.
steps: Find two numbers with product $10$ and sum $-7$: they are $-2$ and $-5$.
Set each factor to zero: $x=2$ or $x=5$.

problems.stem: If $(x-3)^{2}=49$, what is the greatest possible value of $x$?
problems.solution: Taking the square root of both sides keeps both signs: $x-3=\pm 7$. That gives $x=10$ and $x=-4$, and the greatest of these is $10$. Choice A is the other solution, B forgets to add the $3$ back, and D adds $49$ instead of $\sqrt{49}$.
steps: Take square roots of both sides, keeping $\pm$: $x-3=\pm 7$.

problems.stem: If $2x^{2}=50$, what is the positive value of $x$?
problems.solution: Divide by $2$ before taking a root: $x^{2}=25$, so $x=\pm 5$. The question asks only for the positive value, which is why a single grid-in answer is possible; the equation itself still has two solutions.

problems.skill: Sum and product of the roots
problems.stem: What is the sum of the solutions to $x^{2}-9x+14=0$?
problems.solution: By Vieta's formulas the sum of the solutions of $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ is $-b/a$, here $-(-9)/1=9$. No factoring is needed, though factoring confirms it: the roots are $2$ and $7$, whose sum is $9$. Choice A drops the minus sign in $-b/a$, and B and C are the individual roots.
steps: The sum of the roots is $-b/a=9$.
Check: the roots are $2$ and $7$, and $2+7=9$.

problems.skill: Sum and product of the roots
problems.stem: What is the product of the solutions to $(x+4)(x-6)=0$?
problems.solution: The zero-product property gives the solutions $x=-4$ and $x=6$ directly, and their product is $-24$. Choice B is the sum of the roots and D forgets that one root is negative; a factor of $(x+4)$ contributes the root $-4$, not $+4$.
steps: Set each factor to zero: $x=-4$ or $x=6$.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
s = solve((x + 4)*(x - 6), x)
result = s[0]*s[1]

problems.stem: What is the value of the discriminant of the equation $x^{2}+6x+5=0$?
problems.solution: The discriminant is $b^{2}-4ac=6^{2}-4(1)(5)=36-20=16$. Because it is positive, the equation has two distinct real solutions, which matches the factorisation $(x+1)(x+5)=0$. Choice A is $\sqrt{16}$, C forgets the $-4ac$ term entirely, and D adds $4ac$ instead of subtracting it.

problems.stem: Which of the following is a solution to $x^{2}+x-12=0$?
problems.solution: Two numbers with product $-12$ and sum $1$ are $4$ and $-3$, so $x^{2}+x-12=(x+4)(x-3)=0$ and the solutions are $-4$ and $3$. Only $3$ appears among the choices; choice B is the sign-flipped version of the other root, and D is the constant term.
steps: Find two numbers with product $-12$ and sum $1$: they are $4$ and $-3$.
The solutions are $x=-4$ and $x=3$; the listed one is $3$.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
result = max(solve(x**2 + x - 12, x))

problems.stem: The solutions to $x^{2}-6x+4=0$ can be written in the form $3\pm\sqrt{k}$, where $k$ is a positive constant. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: The quadratic formula gives $x=\dfrac{6\pm\sqrt{36-16}}{2}=\dfrac{6\pm\sqrt{20}}{2}=3\pm\sqrt{5}$, since $\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt{5}$ and every term of the numerator is divided by $2$. So $k=5$. Completing the square is just as quick: $(x-3)^{2}=5$.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
s = solve(x**2 - 6*x + 4, x)
result = (max(s) - 3)**2

problems.stem: The equation $x^{2}+8x-3=0$ can be rewritten in the form $(x+4)^{2}=b$, where $b$ is a constant. What is the value of $b$?
problems.solution: Move the constant across first: $x^{2}+8x=3$. Half of $8$ is $4$ and $4^{2}=16$, so adding $16$ to both sides gives $(x+4)^{2}=19$. Choice C adds $16$ only on the left while leaving $-3$ in place, and A flips the sign of the result.
steps: The left side is a perfect square: $(x+4)^{2}=19$, so $b=19$.

problems.skill: Sum and product of the roots
problems.stem: What is the sum of the solutions to $2x^{2}-10x+3=0$?
problems.solution: The sum of the roots is $-b/a=-(-10)/2=5$. The leading coefficient matters here: forgetting to divide by $a=2$ produces choice D. Choice B is the product $c/a$, and A has the sign of $-b/a$ reversed.
steps: The sum of the roots is $-b/a=10/2$.

problems.stem: A ball is kicked from ground level, and its height in feet after $t$ seconds is given by $h=-16t^{2}+48t$. After how many seconds does the ball return to the ground?
problems.solution: The ball is on the ground when $h=0$, so $-16t(t-3)=0$ and $t=0$ or $t=3$. The root $t=0$ is the instant of the kick, so the return happens at $t=3$ seconds. Do not divide the equation by $t$: that would delete the launch time and hide the structure of the problem.
steps: Discard $t=0$ (the kick itself); the ball lands after $3$ seconds.

problems.stem: In the equation $x^{2}+kx+9=0$, $k$ is a positive constant and the equation has exactly one real solution. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: Exactly one real solution means the discriminant is zero: $k^{2}-4(1)(9)=0$, so $k^{2}=36$ and $k=\pm 6$. The condition $k>0$ selects $6$, and indeed $x^{2}+6x+9=(x+3)^{2}$. Choice A is the repeated root, not $k$, and C is the constant term.

problems.stem: What is the smaller of the two solutions to $2x^{2}-7x+3=0$?
problems.solution: Split $-7x$ into parts whose coefficients multiply to $2\cdot 3=6$: $2x^{2}-x-6x+3=x(2x-1)-3(2x-1)=(2x-1)(x-3)$. The solutions are $x=\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $x=3$, and the smaller is $\tfrac{1}{2}$. Choice D is the other root, and C comes from mismatching the factor pair.
steps: Set each factor to zero: $x=\frac{1}{2}$ or $x=3$.

problems.stem: If $(2x-1)^{2}=25$, what is the sum of the possible values of $x$?
problems.solution: Taking square roots gives $2x-1=\pm 5$, so $2x=6$ or $2x=-4$, i.e. $x=3$ or $x=-2$, and the sum is $1$. Choices A and C are the individual solutions, offered to catch a student who stops after one branch of the $\pm$.

problems.stem: The equation $3x^{2}+bx+12=0$ has exactly one real solution, and $b$ is positive. What is the value of $b$?
problems.solution: One real solution means $b^{2}-4ac=0$, so $b^{2}=4(3)(12)=144$ and $b=\pm 12$. Because $b$ is positive, $b=12$; the equation is then $3(x+2)^{2}=0$. The discriminant answers this without ever solving for $x$.

problems.stem: The equation $2x^{2}+12x+5=0$ can be written in the form $2(x+3)^{2}=k$, where $k$ is a constant. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: Factor the $2$ out of the first two terms: $2(x^{2}+6x)+5=0$. Completing the square inside gives $2\big[(x+3)^{2}-9\big]+5=0$, i.e. $2(x+3)^{2}-18+5=0$, so $2(x+3)^{2}=13$. The subtraction of $18$, not $9$, is the step most students miss --- the $2$ multiplies the correction term as well, which is what choice D ignores.

problems.skill: Sum and product of the roots
problems.stem: What is the product of the solutions to $3x^{2}-5x-2=0$?
problems.solution: The product of the roots is $c/a=-2/3$. Factoring confirms it: $(3x+1)(x-2)=0$ gives $x=-\tfrac{1}{3}$ and $x=2$, whose product is $-\tfrac{2}{3}$. Choice B is one of the roots, D is the sum $-b/a$, and C drops the sign of $c$.
steps: The product of the roots is $c/a=-\frac{2}{3}$.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
s = solve(3*x**2 - 5*x - 2, x)
result = s[0]*s[1]

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the graph of $y=x^{2}+6x+c$ intersects the $x$-axis at exactly one point. What is the value of $c$?
problems.solution: Touching the $x$-axis at exactly one point means $x^{2}+6x+c=0$ has exactly one real solution, so $6^{2}-4(1)c=0$ and $c=9$. The parabola is then $y=(x+3)^{2}$, whose vertex $(-3,0)$ sits on the axis. Counting intersections with the $x$-axis is always a discriminant question in disguise.

problems.stem: A rectangular garden is $3$ meters longer than it is wide, and its area is $88$ square meters. What is the width of the garden, in meters?
problems.solution: If the width is $w$, the length is $w+3$ and $w(w+3)=88$, i.e. $w^{2}+3w-88=0$, which factors as $(w+11)(w-8)=0$. The roots are $-11$ and $8$, and a width cannot be negative, so $w=8$. Choice C is the length, and A comes from mis-splitting $88$.
steps: Let the width be $w$; the length is $w+3$.

problems.stem: The solutions to $x^{2}-4x-8=0$ can be written as $a\pm b\sqrt{3}$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers. What is the value of $a+b$?
problems.solution: The quadratic formula gives $x=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{16+32}}{2}=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{48}}{2}$. Since $\sqrt{48}=4\sqrt{3}$, this simplifies to $2\pm 2\sqrt{3}$, so $a=2$, $b=2$ and $a+b=4$. Note that $-4ac=-4(1)(-8)=+32$: a negative $c$ makes the discriminant larger, not smaller.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
s = solve(x**2 - 4*x - 8, x)
a = 2
b = 2
result = a + b if simplify(max(s) - (a + b*sqrt(3))) == 0 else 0

problems.skill: Sum and product of the roots
problems.stem: The solutions to $x^{2}+px+40=0$ are $x=4$ and $x=r$, where $p$ and $r$ are constants. What is the value of $p+r$?
problems.solution: The product of the roots is $c/a=40$, so $4r=40$ and $r=10$. The sum of the roots is $-p$, so $4+10=-p$ and $p=-14$. Therefore $p+r=-14+10=-4$. Choice D reverses the sign of $p$, the single most common slip in this Vieta setup.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
p = -(4 + 10)
rv = 10
result = p + rv if expand((x - 4)*(x - rv)) == expand(x**2 + p*x + 40) else 0

problems.stem: The equation $2x^{2}+8x+k=0$ has no real solutions. Which of the following could be the value of $k$?
problems.solution: No real solutions means a negative discriminant: $8^{2}-4(2)k<0$, so $64<8k$ and $k>8$. Only $10$ satisfies this. The boundary value $k=8$ is deliberately offered: it gives a discriminant of exactly zero, which is one real solution, not none.
problems.verify: result = min([v for v in [2, 4, 8, 10] if 8**2 - 4*2*v < 0])

problems.stem: What is the positive solution to $x^{2}-2x-15=0$?
problems.solution: Two numbers with product $-15$ and sum $-2$ are $-5$ and $3$, so $(x-5)(x+3)=0$ and the solutions are $5$ and $-3$. The positive one is $5$. Choices A and C are those same roots with their signs flipped, the error you make by reading the roots straight out of the parentheses.

problems.stem: If $3x^{2}-27=0$, what is the positive value of $x$?
problems.solution: Isolate the square first: $3x^{2}=27$, so $x^{2}=9$ and $x=\pm 3$. The positive value is $3$. Dividing by $3$ before taking the root keeps the arithmetic clean and avoids a stray $\sqrt{27}$.

problems.stem: How many distinct real solutions does the equation $x^{2}+4x+7=0$ have?
problems.solution: The discriminant is $4^{2}-4(1)(7)=16-28=-12$, which is negative, so there are no real solutions --- the parabola $y=x^{2}+4x+7$ sits entirely above the $x$-axis. A quadratic can never have three solutions, so choice D can be rejected on sight.
steps: Therefore the equation has $0$ real solutions.
problems.verify:
d = 4**2 - 4*1*7
result = 0 if d < 0 else (1 if d == 0 else 2)

problems.stem: The equation $x^{2}+10x+18=0$ can be rewritten as $(x+5)^{2}=c$, where $c$ is a constant. What is the value of $c$?
problems.solution: Move the constant: $x^{2}+10x=-18$. Half of $10$ is $5$ and $5^{2}=25$, so adding $25$ to both sides gives $(x+5)^{2}=-18+25=7$. Choice D adds $25$ to $+18$ instead of $-18$, the sign slip that happens when the constant is not moved across first.

problems.skill: Sum and product of the roots
problems.stem: What is the product of the solutions to $x^{2}+7x-18=0$?
problems.solution: The product of the roots is $c/a=-18/1=-18$; factoring as $(x+9)(x-2)=0$ confirms it, since $(-9)(2)=-18$. Choice D drops the sign of $c$, and B is the sum of the roots, $-b/a=-7$.
steps: The product of the roots is $c/a=-18$.
Check: the roots are $-9$ and $2$, and $(-9)(2)=-18$.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
s = solve(x**2 + 7*x - 18, x)
result = s[0]*s[1]

problems.stem: A stone is thrown from the top of a cliff, and its height in feet after $t$ seconds is $h=-16t^{2}+64t+80$. After how many seconds does the stone hit the ground?
problems.solution: Set $h=0$ and divide by $-16$ to simplify: $t^{2}-4t-5=0$, which factors as $(t-5)(t+1)=0$. The roots are $5$ and $-1$, and only a nonnegative time makes sense, so the stone lands after $5$ seconds. The value $80$ is the cliff's height, not an answer.
steps: Time cannot be negative, so $t=5$ seconds.

problems.stem: What are the solutions to $x^{2}-4x+1=0$?
problems.solution: The quadratic formula gives $x=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{16-4}}{2}=\dfrac{4\pm 2\sqrt{3}}{2}=2\pm\sqrt{3}$. Choice D is what you get by dividing only the first term of the numerator by $2a$, choice C flips the sign of $-b$, and choice B computes the discriminant as $16+4$.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
s = solve(x**2 - 4*x + 1, x)
result = "$2\\pm\\sqrt{3}$" if simplify(max(s) - (2 + sqrt(3))) == 0 else "none"

problems.stem: The length of a rectangular rug is $5$ feet greater than its width, and the rug covers $84$ square feet. What is the width of the rug, in feet?
problems.solution: With width $w$ the area is $w(w+5)=84$, so $w^{2}+5w-84=0$ and $(w+12)(w-7)=0$. The roots are $-12$ and $7$; a width must be positive, so $w=7$ and the length is $12$. Choices A and D are the rejected root and the length, both offered because they appear in correct work.
steps: Let the width be $w$, so the length is $w+5$.

problems.skill: Sum and product of the roots
problems.stem: The solutions to $x^{2}+bx+c=0$ are $-3$ and $5$, where $b$ and $c$ are constants. What is the value of $c$?
problems.solution: A quadratic with those roots is $(x+3)(x-5)=x^{2}-2x-15$, so $c=-15$ (and $b=-2$). Vieta gives the same thing immediately: $c/a$ is the product of the roots, $(-3)(5)=-15$. The sign of $c$ is negative because the roots have opposite signs.
steps: The product of the roots equals $c/a=c$.

problems.stem: The equation $3x^{2}-12x+5=0$ can be written in the form $3(x-2)^{2}=k$, where $k$ is a constant. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: Factor $3$ from the first two terms: $3(x^{2}-4x)+5=0$. Completing the square inside gives $3\big[(x-2)^{2}-4\big]+5=0$, so $3(x-2)^{2}-12+5=0$ and $3(x-2)^{2}=7$. The correction term is $3\cdot 4=12$, not $4$; using $4$ produces choice A.

problems.stem: In the equation $kx^{2}+12x+9=0$, $k$ is a nonzero constant and the equation has exactly one real solution. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: Exactly one real solution means $b^{2}-4ac=0$, here $12^{2}-4k(9)=144-36k=0$, so $k=4$. The equation becomes $4x^{2}+12x+9=(2x+3)^{2}=0$. Choice C comes from halving $12$ and choice A from the perfect-square constant.

problems.stem: A rocket's height in feet after $t$ seconds is $h=-16t^{2}+96t$. What is the smaller of the two values of $t$ at which the height is $128$ feet?
problems.solution: Set $-16t^{2}+96t=128$ and divide by $-16$: $t^{2}-6t+8=0$, so $(t-2)(t-4)=0$ and $t=2$ or $t=4$. Both times are physically real --- the rocket passes $128$ feet on the way up at $t=2$ and again on the way down at $t=4$ --- and the smaller is $2$.

problems.stem: What is the positive difference between the two solutions to $x^{2}-6x+2=0$?
problems.solution: The formula gives $x=\dfrac{6\pm\sqrt{36-8}}{2}=\dfrac{6\pm 2\sqrt{7}}{2}=3\pm\sqrt{7}$, so the difference is $(3+\sqrt{7})-(3-\sqrt{7})=2\sqrt{7}$. The distance between the roots is always twice the square-root part, which is why choice A --- the square-root part alone --- is wrong.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
s = solve(x**2 - 6*x + 2, x)
result = "$2\\sqrt{7}$" if simplify(max(s) - min(s) - 2*sqrt(7)) == 0 else "none"

problems.stem: For which of the following values of $k$ does the equation $x^{2}+kx+4=0$ have two distinct real solutions?
problems.solution: Two distinct real solutions require $k^{2}-16>0$, that is $|k|>4$. Only $k=5$ qualifies. The value $k=4$ gives a discriminant of exactly zero --- a single repeated root, $(x+2)^{2}=0$ --- which is the trap in this item.
problems.verify: result = max([v for v in [0, 2, 4, 5] if v**2 - 16 > 0])

problems.skill: Sum and product of the roots
problems.stem: What is the sum of the solutions to $4x^{2}-20x+9=0$?
problems.solution: The sum of the roots is $-b/a=20/4=5$; factoring as $(2x-1)(2x-9)=0$ gives $\tfrac12+\tfrac92=5$. Choice A is the product $c/a$, choice B is $-b/(4a)$ from dividing by $2a$ twice, and D forgets to divide by $a$ at all.
steps: The sum of the roots is $-b/a=20/4$.

problems.skill: Sum and product of the roots
problems.stem: If $x^{2}+6x=16$, what is the sum of all possible values of $x$?
problems.solution: Vieta applies only in standard form, so rewrite as $x^{2}+6x-16=0$; the sum of the roots is then $-b/a=-6$. Factoring confirms it: $(x+8)(x-2)=0$ gives $-8$ and $2$, whose sum is $-6$. Choices A and B are pieces of that work mistaken for the whole answer.
steps: The sum of the roots is $-b/a=-6$.
Check: the roots are $-8$ and $2$, and $-8+2=-6$.

problems.stem: If $\dfrac{12}{x}=x-1$ and $x\neq 0$, what is the greatest possible value of $x$?
problems.solution: Multiply both sides by $x$: $12=x^{2}-x$, so $x^{2}-x-12=0$ and $(x-4)(x+3)=0$. The solutions are $4$ and $-3$, both valid since neither is $0$, and the greatest is $4$. Multiplying through by the variable is the standard move that turns a rational equation into a quadratic one.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
result = max(solve(x**2 - x - 12, x))

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the line $y=2x+3$ intersects the parabola $y=x^{2}+k$ at exactly one point, where $k$ is a constant. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: Setting the expressions equal gives $x^{2}+k=2x+3$, i.e. $x^{2}-2x+(k-3)=0$. One point of intersection means one real solution, so the discriminant vanishes: $4-4(k-3)=0$, giving $k-3=1$ and $k=4$. The line is then tangent to the parabola at $(1,5)$.

problems.skill: Sum and product of the roots
problems.stem: The equation $x^{2}-14x+k=0$ has two positive integer solutions that differ by $4$. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: The two roots add to $-b/a=14$ and differ by $4$, so they are $9$ and $5$. Their product is $c/a=k$, giving $k=45$. Setting up sum and difference together is faster than guessing factor pairs of an unknown constant.
steps: The roots sum to $14$ and differ by $4$.

problems.stem: A ball is launched from a platform, and its height in feet after $t$ seconds is $h=-16t^{2}+40t+24$. After how many seconds does the ball hit the ground?
problems.solution: Set $h=0$ and divide by $-8$: $2t^{2}-5t-3=0$, which factors as $(2t+1)(t-3)=0$. The roots are $-\tfrac12$ and $3$; a negative time is impossible, so the ball lands after $3$ seconds. Choice A is the time at the vertex, $-b/(2a)$, which is when the ball is highest, not when it lands.
steps: Reject $t=-\frac{1}{2}$; the ball lands at $t=3$ seconds.

problems.stem: The solutions to $2x^{2}-8x+3=0$ can be written as $\dfrac{a\pm\sqrt{b}}{2}$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers. What is the value of $a+b$?
problems.solution: The formula gives $x=\dfrac{8\pm\sqrt{64-24}}{4}=\dfrac{8\pm\sqrt{40}}{4}=\dfrac{8\pm 2\sqrt{10}}{4}=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{10}}{2}$, so $a=4$, $b=10$ and $a+b=14$. Choice B stops at the unsimplified $\dfrac{8\pm\sqrt{40}}{4}$ and reads off $8$ and $10$; choice C reads off $4$ and $40$.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
s = solve(2*x**2 - 8*x + 3, x)
a = 4
b = 10
result = a + b if simplify(max(s) - (a + sqrt(b))/2) == 0 else 0

problems.stem: The equation $x^{2}+kx+k+3=0$ has exactly one real solution. What is the sum of all possible values of $k$?
problems.solution: One real solution means the discriminant is zero: $k^{2}-4(1)(k+3)=0$, i.e. $k^{2}-4k-12=0$, which factors as $(k-6)(k+2)=0$. So $k=6$ or $k=-2$, and their sum is $4$. Vieta on the equation in $k$ gives the same total in one step: the sum is $-(-4)/1=4$. Choice D is only one of the two values.
